entity.name: Francisco Goya
entity.description: The court painter who went deaf and started painting nightmares. Francisco Goya rose from a provincial Aragonese family to become Spain's Prime Court Painter, then produced The Third of May 1808 and the terrifying Black Paintings on his own walls. Often called the last Old Master and the first modern artist.

story.name: Francisco Goya
story.description: Tapestry cartoons for the royal palace, a mysterious illness that causes deafness, The Third of May 1808 capturing Napoleon's horrors, and Black Paintings on his own walls in isolation.

moments.name: Francisco Goya Is Born in a Small Aragonese Village
moments.subtitle: A gilder's son from a modest brick cottage who will become Spain's greatest painter
moments.description: On March 30, 1746, Francisco Jose de Goya y Lucientes was born in Fuendetodos, a small village in Aragon, Spain. His father Jose was a gilder of Basque origin who specialized in religious craftwork; his mother's family had modest pretensions of nobility. The family had moved temporarily from Zaragoza, likely for a work commission. Around 1749, the Goyas returned to Zaragoza, where young Francisco began his education and formed a lifelong friendship with schoolmate Martin Zapater — their 131 surviving letters provide invaluable insight into Goya's early career. From these humble provincial beginnings, Goya would rise to become the most important Spanish artist of his era.

moments.name: Goya Becomes Spain's Prime Court Painter — the Highest Rank Possible
moments.subtitle: The portraits he paints of the royal family are so unflattering they might be satire
moments.description: In 1799, Francisco Goya was appointed Primer Pintor de Camara (Prime Court Painter), the most prestigious position available to a Spanish artist, with a salary of 50,000 reales and a coach allowance. His path to this honor had begun in 1786 when he first became a court painter to Charles III. In 1800-01, Goya painted Charles IV of Spain and His Family, a group portrait so brutally honest that modern interpreters read it as deliberate satire — placing the domineering Queen Louisa at the center and hiding a painting of Lot and his daughters in the background. Goya embedded himself in the composition, observing from the shadows, just as Velazquez had done 150 years earlier in Las Meninas.

moments.name: Goya Paints The Third of May 1808 — War Art's Most Famous Image
moments.subtitle: A deaf painter creates the defining image of Napoleonic brutality six years after the event
moments.description: In 1814, Francisco Goya painted The Third of May 1808, depicting the execution of Spanish civilians by Napoleon's soldiers in Madrid. The painting shows a man in a white shirt, arms flung wide in a Christ-like pose, facing a firing squad by lantern light. Goya had witnessed the French occupation of Madrid firsthand beginning in 1808, and the horrors of the Peninsular War haunted him for years — he also produced the Disasters of War etching series documenting wartime atrocities. The Third of May broke every convention of military painting: there are no heroes, no glory, only terror. The work influenced Manet, Picasso, and virtually every anti-war artist who followed.

moments.name: A Deaf Goya Paints Nightmares Directly onto His Own Walls
moments.subtitle: Saturn devouring his son and other horrors, never meant for public eyes
moments.description: Between 1819 and 1823, Francisco Goya — now deaf, elderly, and disillusioned — painted 14 works directly onto the plaster walls of his country house outside Madrid, known as the Quinta del Sordo (House of the Deaf Man). These Black Paintings, including the iconic Saturn Devouring His Son, depict witches, monsters, and scenes of madness in dark, visceral brushstrokes. Goya never titled or explained them, and they were never intended for public display. The paintings were transferred to canvas in 1874 and donated to the Museo del Prado. They represent one of the most radical artistic statements in Western art — the private visions of a genius confronting mortality and despair.

moments.name: Francisco Goya Dies in Exile in Bordeaux at Age 82
moments.subtitle: Spain's greatest painter spends his final years as a voluntary exile in France
moments.description: On April 16, 1828, Francisco Goya died in Bordeaux, France, at the age of 82, following a stroke that left him paralyzed on his right side. Goya had left Spain in 1824, disillusioned by the repressive political climate under King Ferdinand VII, and settled in Bordeaux with his much younger companion Leocadia Weiss. Even in exile, he continued working — completing his La Tauromaquia series and experimenting with the new medium of lithography. Goya was buried in Bordeaux, but his remains were later transferred to Madrid. When the coffin was opened, the skull was missing — it has never been found. His body now rests in the San Antonio de la Florida chapel in Madrid.
